title: Supervision 1 essay
description: Discuss, with examples, why negative feedback mechanisms are more common than positive feedback mechanisms in animal physiology.
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 1. Write it here in one sitting, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

Why write it like this? Your BMS exams are taken on a computer, in an online exam system. If you write your supervision essays the same way, typed in one go without notes and without pasting anything in, the exam will feel familiar when it comes. Writing this way also lets your supervisor see how you write under exam conditions, and that’s what the feedback is about.

  • Time. There’s no time limit, but give yourself about 40 minutes. The clock at the top counts the time you spend writing and tells you when you reach 40 minutes. Spend the first few minutes planning, on paper if you like.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your essay, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture from your computer, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your essay.
  • Saving. Your essay is saved in this browser as you type, so you can leave and come back to it.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the last tile at the bottom), check your essay and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Negative and positive feedback
questions.text:
Discuss, with examples, why negative feedback mechanisms are more common than positive feedback mechanisms in animal physiology.

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Use examples from the lectures, and explain how each one supports your argument.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it to look back over what you wrote before the supervision. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers, and the questions it should ask.

What the title asks. “Why” asks for an explanation and an argument, not a list of feedback loops. “With examples” asks for specific, accurate examples, each one linked to the point it supports. “Discuss” invites you to weigh up the claim. In what sense is negative feedback “more common”, and are there complications?

  • Definitions. In negative feedback, a sensor detects a change in a regulated variable, the change is compared with a set point, and the error signal drives a response (an effector) that opposes it. In positive feedback the response reinforces the change. It helps to tell regulated variables apart from controlled ones.
  • Negative feedback is stabilising, and homeostasis needs stability. Cells only work within a narrow range of conditions, so the internal environment (Claude Bernard’s milieu intérieur) has to be held relatively constant against disturbances. Good examples are core temperature, plasma osmolarity (osmoreceptors, ADH and thirst), blood glucose (insulin and glucagon), arterial pressure (the baroreceptor reflex), and the hormone axes, such as the long-loop feedback of cortisol on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, or of thyroid hormones on TRH and TSH.
  • Positive feedback is unstable. Left to itself it runs away, so it can’t hold a variable steady. It’s used where a fast, all-or-none or self-completing change is needed, and something always brings it to an end. Examples include the rising phase of the action potential (ended by Na⁺-channel inactivation and K⁺ channels), parturition and the Ferguson reflex (oxytocin, ended by delivery), urination, blood clotting (limited by anticoagulant mechanisms) and the LH surge before ovulation.
  • So positive feedback is usually brief, and it’s embedded in systems that are otherwise under negative feedback. That’s part of the reason it’s less common.
  • Evaluation. Negative feedback has its limits. It only acts once an error has appeared, and with a delay it overshoots and oscillates, as in the drinking problem from the first lecture. Feed-forward control helps here. Receptors in the mouth and stomach switch off thirst before the water has been absorbed (Bellows, 1938), and circadian rhythms prepare the body for predictable daily events. Set points can also move (in fever, or with the daily rhythm of body temperature), not every animal regulates every variable (think of conformers such as the naked mole-rat), and “more common” is hard to count. You could even point out that the circadian clock is a negative feedback loop that’s built, with a long delay, to oscillate.

Against the core criteria. Does each paragraph make clear how its example helps to answer the “why”? Do you take a position early on and build on it? Do you assess your examples (how strong and how typical they are) rather than just describing them? Does the conclusion pull the argument together?
